summary: Describes how to produce RSA/SHA-1 signature records and RSA key records in the Domain Name System. It completely replaces RFC 2537 for RSA keys. These records let DNS data be signed and verified in DNSSEC.

eli5.summary: It explains how to put a tamper-proof stamp on address-book entries so you can tell nobody changed them.

questions: how to publish rsa keys in dnssec
what is rsa sha1 in dns
why was rsa md5 replaced in dnssec
subtitle: How DNS stores RSA public keys and RSA/SHA-1 signatures, replacing the weaker MD5-based scheme.

tldr.problem: The earlier DNS scheme for RSA signatures (RFC 2537) used the MD5 hash, and research had revealed hints of weakness in MD5.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3110 defines SIG records that sign a SHA-1 hash with RSA, and restates how to store RSA public keys in KEY records, both under algorithm number 5.
tldr.outcome: RSA with SHA-1 became mandatory for DNSSEC and RSA/MD5 signing was marked NOT RECOMMENDED. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2537 and is updated by RFC 6944.

today: RFC 3110 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2537 and is updated by RFC 6944. Check that update for the current state of the algorithm.

sections.title: Why MD5 Was Replaced
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) had been extended with digital signatures and cryptographic keys, so DNS data could be secured and used to distribute keys. RFC 2537 described how to store RSA keys and RSA/MD5 signatures in the DNS.

Since then, cryptographic research had revealed hints of weakness in the MD5 hash. SHA-1 produces a larger hash and was by then generally acknowledged to be stronger. The RFC says a stronger hash is probably not needed today in most secure zones, but that critical zones such as the root, most top level domains and some second and third level domains are valuable enough targets that it would be negligent not to offer it.

It also notes that the extra computation for SHA-1 compared with MD5 is insignificant next to the RSA modular exponentiation.
sections.eli5: The old way of making a fingerprint of a message was starting to look a bit weak. A stronger fingerprint costs almost nothing extra, so it is worth switching.

sections.title: What the RFC Changes and Requires
sections.content:
The document describes how to produce RSA/SHA1 SIG resource records and, so that it completely replaces RFC 2537, also how to produce RSA KEY records. The algorithm number of the RSA KEY record is changed to match the new signature algorithm. No other changes are made to DNS security.

Two requirements are stated up front. Implementing RSA with SHA1 in DNS is MANDATORY for DNSSEC, and generating RSA/MD5 SIG records as described in RFC 2537 is NOT RECOMMENDED. The use of the earlier, weaker mechanism is deprecated.
sections.eli5: The rule is simple: use the new stronger stamp, and please stop using the old one.

sections.title: RSA Public KEY Records
sections.content:
RSA public keys are stored in the DNS as KEY records with algorithm number 5. The algorithm-specific part of the record data holds three things in order: the exponent length (1 or 3 octets), the exponent itself, and the modulus, which takes the remaining space.

The exponent length is one octet if the exponent is 1 to 255 octets long. If it is longer than 255 octets, it is a zero octet followed by a two-octet unsigned length. The modulus length is not stored; it is worked out from RDLENGTH and the fields before it. Leading zero octets are prohibited in both the exponent and the modulus.

For interoperability, the exponent and modulus are each limited to 4096 bits. KEY records used with RSA/SHA1 signatures MUST use algorithm number 5 rather than the number from the obsoleted RFC 2537.
sections.eli5: A public key is stored as a short note: first how long one number is, then that number, then the rest, which is a second number. Keeping the layout fixed means everybody reads it the same way.

sections.title: RSA/SHA1 SIG Records
sections.content:
RSA/SHA1 signatures are stored in SIG records, also with algorithm number 5. The data to be signed is determined as in RFC 2535. The signer first computes hash = SHA1 ( data ) and then the signature as ( 01 | FF* | 00 | prefix | hash ) ** e (mod n).

Here | is concatenation, e is the signer's private key exponent and n is the modulus of the signer's public key. The octets 01, FF and 00 are fixed. The prefix is the ASN.1 BER SHA1 algorithm designator prefix from PKCS1, which is hex 30 21 30 09 06 05 2B 0E 03 02 1A 05 00 04 14. It is included to make it easier to use standard cryptographic libraries. These specifications are identical to the corresponding parts of PKCS #1.

The FF octet MUST be repeated the maximum number of times such that the value being exponentiated is one octet shorter than n. The size of n MUST be not less than 512 bits and not more than 4096 bits, and n and e SHOULD be chosen so the public exponent is small. Leading zero bytes are permitted in the signature.
sections.eli5: The signer shrinks the message to a fingerprint, pads it out in a fixed way, and locks it with a secret number. Anyone with the matching public number can check the lock.

sections.title: Performance Considerations
sections.content:
Signature generation speeds are roughly the same for RSA and DSA, and with enough pre-computation DSA is faster. Key generation is also faster for DSA. But verifying a signature is an order of magnitude slower with DSA when the RSA public exponent is small, which is the recommended choice for KEY records used to authenticate DNS data.

A public exponent of 3 minimizes the effort to verify a signature. It is weak for confidentiality, because the same data encrypted under three different keys with exponent 3 can be recovered using the Chinese Remainder Theorem. That is acceptable for keys used only for authentication, as in DNSSEC. For keys that might later serve other uses, a more conservative choice is 65537.

The RFC also notes that DNS implementations are optimized for transfers typically under 512 bytes, so it is advisable to keep KEY record sets small consistent with adequate security. A secure zone also returns at least one SIG record alongside them.
sections.eli5: A small secret-lock number makes checking fast. That is fine when you only need to prove who sent something, but not when you need to keep a message private.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
For IANA, DNSSEC algorithm number 5 is allocated for both RSA/SHA1 SIG records and RSA KEY records.

Many of the security considerations in RFC 2535 apply. Keys retrieved from the DNS should not be trusted unless they were securely obtained from a secure resolver or independently verified by the user, and that process meets the user's security policies. How strong a key needs to be depends on local policy, and for critical applications implementers should consider the range of algorithms and key sizes. The RFC points to RFC 2541 for operational advice.
sections.eli5: Do not trust a key just because it showed up. Make sure you got it from a safe source, and pick a strong enough lock for important things.

data.title: RSA/SHA1 signature
data.code:
hash = SHA1 ( data )

signature = ( 01 | FF* | 00 | prefix | hash ) ** e (mod n)

prefix = hex 30 21 30 09 06 05 2B 0E 03 02 1A 05 00 04 14
